topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; frameworks and competencies may require adaptation for Australian healthcare systems, different regulatory environments, and workforce structures.
takeaways: Competency frameworks for digital health typically span technical skills, data literacy, and change management—use this multi-domain approach when designing AI capability-building programmes for health sector employees.

European public health contexts emphasise regulatory compliance and interoperability; Australian organisations should map these competencies against local standards (e.g., NHMRC guidelines, state health department requirements) rather than directly importing frameworks.

Scoping reviews identify breadth of existing frameworks but not depth of implementation effectiveness; supplement this with local evidence or pilot testing before rolling out competency programmes across your organisation.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focused on faculty development in public health education contexts. Findings may not generalise to other sectors or non-academic settings, and geographic scope is unclear from the snippet provided.
takeaways: Structured faculty development programmes can shift mindsets from AI resistance to engagement; consider designing train-the-trainer initiatives to build internal capacity before rolling out AI literacy to learners.

Public health educators face unique barriers to AI adoption (e.g., concerns about job displacement, unfamiliar terminology); tailor AI literacy programmes to address sector-specific anxieties and use case examples relevant to public health practice.
Faculty readiness is a prerequisite for effective AI literacy delivery — invest in upskilling educators themselves before expecting them to teach AI concepts to their students or teams.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to middle school context; applicability to adult workforce development in Australia depends on whether frameworks designed for younger learners transfer to professional settings. Geographic scope unclear from snippet.
takeaways: Holistic digital literacy frameworks that embed AI competencies (not isolated AI training) may provide a stronger foundation for learners to understand AI's role across domains—consider whether your organisation's AI upskilling mirrors this integrated approach rather than treating AI as a standalone module.

Middle school curricula offer insights into foundational AI concepts and competencies; audit your current employee induction or onboarding to check whether basic AI literacy concepts (e.g., how algorithms work, bias in AI systems) are explicitly taught or assumed.

articles.title: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to be a conceptual discourse rather than empirical research, so findings are illustrative rather than evidence-based. Applicability depends on whether examples are drawn from specific healthcare systems or are generalised.
takeaways: When implementing AI in care settings, actively design for person-centredness by ensuring AI systems support rather than replace human judgment and individualised decision-making.
Identify and document potential pitfalls (bias, depersonalisation, over-reliance on automation) before deployment to build safeguards into AI literacy programs for care teams.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet alone, but findings on higher education AI competency development may have limited direct application to workplace training in organisations outside academia, though pedagogical principles could transfer.
takeaways: Identify which specific AI competencies (technical, ethical, domain-specific) are most relevant to your organisation's roles, rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all higher education model.

Consider how university-based strategies for AI literacy (e.g. capstone projects, interdisciplinary collaboration) could be adapted to your workplace context, including integration with existing professional development structures.

articles.title: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design - Frontiers
articles.snippet: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on materials-informatics education context; applicability to other domains or general workplace AI literacy programmes unclear without full article details.
takeaways: Design AI literacy curricula around actual workflows rather than abstract concepts — embedding AI learning within domain-specific tasks (here: materials science) improves relevance and retention.

Integrate scientific judgment and equity considerations into AI literacy frameworks from the start, not as add-ons; this ensures learners develop critical evaluation skills alongside technical understanding.
Use a structured curriculum design approach that maps learning objectives to real application contexts, helping learners understand when and how to apply AI tools appropriately in their field.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be fully assessed from the title and snippet alone; the full paper would clarify sample size, sectors, and geographic scope. The conceptual framework of 'double-edged' AI adoption effects likely has broad relevance across knowledge-work contexts, but empirical findings may be limited by specific industry or organisational contexts studied.
takeaways: AI adoption can simultaneously enhance and constrain employee creativity depending on implementation approach — screen for whether your organisation is using AI to augment creative thinking versus replace human judgment.

Consider designing AI integration initiatives with explicit attention to preserving creative autonomy and exploration; unmanaged AI adoption may inadvertently reduce experimentation and novel idea generation among staff.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings apply primarily to nursing contexts where medical AI is being implemented. Generalisability to other professions or non-healthcare sectors is unclear without additional detail on sample composition and geographic location.
takeaways: When introducing AI tools to clinical teams, prioritise maintaining or expanding nurses' decision-making autonomy — AI readiness alone won't improve wellbeing if staff feel their autonomy is diminished.

Design AI implementation programmes that explicitly address how technology will support (rather than replace) clinical judgment; this autonomy preservation appears critical for staff wellbeing outcomes.
Measure work autonomy alongside AI readiness metrics during rollout to identify early whether staff feel their professional agency is protected.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone. The snippet provides insufficient detail about sample size, geography, sector, or methodology to evaluate the breadth of findings.
takeaways: AI-enabled work systems create dual pathways to employee wellbeing — some employees experience strain (e.g. from increased monitoring or skill gaps) while others gain resources (e.g. reduced drudgery, autonomy); tailor your AI implementation approach to mitigate strain and amplify resource gains for different employee groups.

The relationship between AI adoption and wellbeing is not uniformly positive or negative; assess your workforce's specific responses to identify which employees are experiencing strain versus resource benefits, then design targeted interventions accordingly.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, the geographic scope and sample characteristics cannot be determined. Generalisability depends on sector coverage, sample size, and whether the study was conducted in a single country or multiple regions.
takeaways: Role ambiguity around AI use is a key barrier to effective employee-AI collaboration; clarity about expected AI responsibilities and decision-making authority can unlock adoption.
Self-efficacy with AI tools directly influences how employees engage with generative AI; targeted training and early wins build confidence and reduce hesitation.

Organizations should address both structural (role clarity) and individual (confidence-building) factors in parallel when implementing generative AI, as these dual pathways interact to shape collaboration outcomes.

articles.title: Human future traits and cultural equity in AI-augmented work: a multilevel psychological framework for human value creation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Human future traits and cultural equity in AI-augmented work: a multilevel psychological framework for human value creation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a theoretical framework rather than empirical validation. Applicability depends on how well the multilevel model translates across different organisational contexts, sectors, and cultural settings. Framework development is typically generic, but real-world effectiveness would need testing in specific workplace environments.
takeaways: Use the multilevel psychological framework to audit which human traits your organisation is cultivating in AI-augmented roles — consider whether you're developing adaptability, creative problem-solving, and emotional intelligence alongside technical AI literacy.

Embed cultural equity considerations into AI capability development programmes; identify potential cultural biases in how AI augmentation might advantage some employee groups over others, and design interventions to ensure equitable access to AI upskilling and career progression.

Map 'human value creation' touchpoints across individual, team, and organisational levels when rolling out AI tools — this helps identify where human strengths complement AI capabilities rather than viewing automation as pure replacement.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be particularly relevant to organizations with paternalistic leadership structures, which are more common in collectivist cultures (e.g., East Asia). Generalisability to Western individualistic organizational contexts with different leadership styles requires caution.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees — those who feel a sense of ownership are more likely to actively collaborate with and customize AI systems to fit their work needs.

In paternalistic leadership contexts, leaders can encourage 'AI crafting' (personalizing and adapting AI tools) as a mechanism to deepen employee engagement with AI, bridging the gap between top-down AI adoption and bottom-up employee agency.

Recognize that the relationship between ownership, AI crafting, and collaboration may operate differently across organizational cultures — test these mechanisms in your specific context before scaling organization-wide AI initiatives.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's framework reflects their consulting experience with large organisations, but lacks empirical validation across sectors or geographies. Applicability may vary depending on organisation size, industry, and existing change management maturity.
takeaways: Shift from 'adoption' framing (compliance-focused) to 'adaptation' framing (behaviour-change focused) — this reframes AI integration as building new capabilities rather than implementing a tool, which can improve engagement and sustained behaviour change.

Design change interventions around the specific human behaviours AI requires, rather than around technology rollout timelines — identify which team behaviours need to shift (e.g., how decisions are made, how data is interpreted) before selecting change tactics.

Address the gap between policy and practice: many organisations announce AI strategies but fail to reinforce the daily behaviours needed to make them work — embed behavioural expectations into role design, feedback systems, and team norms.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a perspective piece from Stanford GSB without specified empirical sample or geographic scope. Insights may reflect US business school viewpoint and may not generalise to Australian workplace contexts or non-English speaking regions.
takeaways: Identify specific roles in your organisation most vulnerable to AI displacement and design upskilling programs now, rather than waiting for disruption to occur.
Frame AI adoption internally as a tool augmenting human capability rather than replacing workers — this messaging can reduce resistance and support psychological safety during organisational change.
Establish clear communication channels about how AI will reshape job roles and career progression to mitigate uncertainty-driven disengagement among employees.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry surveys, likely skewed toward large enterprises in developed economies. Findings may not apply to small-to-medium businesses or resource-constrained organisations.
takeaways: Structure AI transformation into distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) to set realistic timelines and milestones — organisations that conflate these stages often underestimate the effort required to move beyond pilot projects.

Use the 'three horizons' framework to identify which capability gaps need addressing at each stage, helping teams prioritise behaviour change and capability-building interventions matched to their current transformation phase rather than attempting all changes simultaneously.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings apply to understanding how AI awareness influences employee behaviour through stress appraisal and resource-demand dynamics, though generalisability depends on sample characteristics and organisational context not evident from the title.
takeaways: Design AI awareness interventions that account for how employees cognitively appraise AI as a threat or opportunity — those perceiving AI as a challenge requiring upskilling may engage in constructive job crafting, while threat appraisals may trigger defensive responses.

Use the Job Demands-Resources framework to structure AI change initiatives: ensure adequate training resources and autonomy support alongside AI adoption, as unbalanced demands without resources will reduce job crafting engagement.

Monitor two distinct pathways: employees may craft their roles either by building new AI-related skills (active adaptation) or by narrowing responsibilities (withdrawal) — target interventions to encourage the former through transparent communication about role evolution.

articles.title: Innovative technologies and workplace collaborations in the energy sector based in the United Arab Emirates - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Innovative technologies and workplace collaborations in the energy sector based in the United Arab Emirates  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to the UAE energy sector and may not generalise to other geographic regions, industries, or cultural contexts. The snippet provides insufficient detail to assess methodological rigour or sample size.
takeaways: Examine how technology adoption in your workplace is framed to teams — positioning it as a collaboration enabler (rather than a replacement tool) may increase engagement and behaviour change acceptance in your organisation.

Consider whether workplace collaboration structures in your sector are aligned with the technologies you're introducing; misalignment often undermines technology uptake and sustainable behaviour change.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on BCG's consulting experience across sectors and geographies, but findings reflect organisations with resources for large-scale AI transformation programmes; applicability may be lower for small-to-medium enterprises or resource-constrained settings.
takeaways: Link AI capability development directly to workforce transformation strategy: organisations must align upskilling programmes, role redesign, and organisational culture shifts with AI adoption, not treat them as separate initiatives.

Identify and address the 'capability gap' early by assessing current workforce skills against AI-enabled roles, then design targeted learning pathways and hire strategically to close gaps before implementation.

Create feedback loops between frontline teams and AI implementation leaders to surface adoption barriers and refine change management approaches in real time, rather than relying on top-down rollout plans.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on established psychological research on social connection and health outcomes across diverse populations.
takeaways: Strong friendships reduce stress hormones and boost immune function in measurable ways — it's not just feeling good, it's biology at work.
The quality of friendships matters far more than quantity; even one close, supportive relationship can have significant health benefits.
Social isolation carries health risks comparable to smoking or obesity, making friendship surprisingly powerful medicine for longevity and wellbeing.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — news reports typically summarize research findings without full methodological details; actual study scope and sample characteristics unclear from snippet alone.
takeaways: Personality traits appear to have a stronger genetic component than previously thought, challenging the nature-nurture balance scientists had estimated.

This finding is counterintuitive because it suggests we're 'hardwired' in ways we didn't fully appreciate—which might explain why people's core traits feel so stubbornly consistent across their lives.
It's fascinating for anyone wondering why their quirks feel so 'just like me'—there's now evidence that's not just habit or upbringing, but genuinely baked into your biology.

articles.title: Personality traits in musicians with different types of music performance anxiety - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Personality traits in musicians with different types of music performance anxiety  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a single study on musicians experiencing performance anxiety; generalisability depends on sample size and geographic scope, which are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Musicians with performance anxiety show distinct personality profiles depending on the type of anxiety they experience — suggesting that 'stage fright' isn't one-size-fits-all, and different triggers may correlate with different temperaments.

This finding is a nice reminder that anxiety isn't purely situational; personality traits play a measurable role in how people respond to high-pressure performance, which could explain why some performers thrive on the spotlight while others struggle with identical circumstances.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — appears to draw on large-scale cross-cultural data, suggesting personality-music links hold across diverse populations and regions.
takeaways: Your taste in music might be a more reliable personality marker than you'd expect — suggesting our playlists reveal something genuinely universal about who we are, not just our local culture.

Personality traits and musical preferences appear connected worldwide, implying that humans across radically different cultures share underlying similarities in how they experience and respond to sound.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises psychological research on true crime appeal, but geographic scope of underlying studies not specified in snippet; likely skews toward Western populations given typical criminology research patterns.
takeaways: True crime obsession isn't morbid voyeurism — it taps into genuine psychological needs like sense-making, control, and safety-seeking in an uncertain world.
The appeal crosses demographics in surprising ways; it's not just 'dark' entertainment but how people process risk and develop crime-prevention awareness.
Binge-watching true crime gives viewers a paradoxical sense of mastery: they solve puzzles and catch perpetrators from their couch, satisfying problem-solving drives without real danger.

articles.title: Which Personality Traits Are Most Important to Employers? - Association for Psychological Science – APS
articles.snippet: Which Personality Traits Are Most Important to Employers?  Association for Psychological Science – APS
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises employer perspectives on personality traits, but specific geographic scope and sample composition unclear from title/snippet alone.
takeaways: Employers prioritise certain personality traits over others when hiring — this research reveals which ones actually matter most in practice, not just which ones sound good on job applications.

The gap between which traits employers say they value and which ones actually predict job performance can be surprising — intuition about 'ideal' personalities often doesn't match real-world outcomes.
Understanding employer priorities gives an interesting window into workplace culture: what gets rewarded tells us a lot about how organisations actually operate versus how they present themselves.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on the specific sample used (likely organisational teams), but geographic scope and sector details are not provided in the snippet, limiting assessment of how broadly these relationships apply across different cultural contexts and industries.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership directly strengthens team psychological safety, which in turn drives innovation — prioritise creating psychologically safe environments where team members feel valued and heard as a mechanism for fostering creative contributions.

Leaders' power distance orientation (their comfort with hierarchical distance) moderates this relationship — consider assessing your own cultural assumptions about hierarchy and authority, as leaders with lower power distance orientation may be more effective at combining inclusive behaviours with psychological safety.

Design leadership interventions that explicitly connect inclusive practices to innovation outcomes; teams may not automatically link feeling safe to generating novel ideas, so help leaders frame psychological safety as a foundation for risk-taking and creative thinking.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited without full access to methodology details. Cross-sectional design cannot establish causation. Results depend on sample characteristics (sector, geography, organisation size) which are not clear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent investment in psychological safety and ethical leadership can trigger depression and mental health risks among employees — assess your current psychological safety baseline before scaling AI initiatives.

Ethical leadership is a critical protective factor during AI transitions; leaders should explicitly model trustworthy AI decision-making and create forums where employees can voice concerns about AI implementation without fear of repercussion.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but the article does not specify sample size, study design, or geographic scope of evidence. Findings likely most applicable to large, multinational organisations.
takeaways: Create explicit team norms and check-ins that invite quieter voices into discussions; psychological safety reduces participation gaps between dominant and marginalised employee groups.
Train leaders to model vulnerability and reward dissent or questions without status consequences; this shifts perceived risk of speaking up and increases inclusivity in idea generation.

Measure psychological safety regularly (e.g. via pulse surveys or team retrospectives) as a diagnostic tool — teams with low scores often show poor cross-functional collaboration and lower innovation metrics.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — PwC surveys typically capture large, diverse global samples across sectors and geographies, though response bias toward white-collar and developed economies is common. Results reflect 2026 workforce sentiment but may not represent all worker populations equally.
takeaways: Use survey findings to benchmark your organisation's psychological safety climate against global peer expectations — identify gaps where employee hopes (e.g., inclusion, autonomy, job security) are not being met.

Monitor which workforce 'fears' are prevalent in your sector and organisation; tailor safety interventions (e.g., transparent communication, skill development, flexible work arrangements) to address the specific anxieties most likely to undermine trust and voice.

Compare results across demographic groups within your workforce to surface where psychological safety may be unevenly distributed — this can reveal which teams or populations need targeted support to feel equally safe speaking up.

articles.title: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to synthesize existing research on AI and workforce dynamics, but geographic scope and specific organisational contexts are not detailed in the title/snippet provided.
takeaways: Co-skilling programmes (pairing AI technical training with soft skills development) help employees build confidence in AI-driven roles and reduce psychological threat, which supports psychological safety in teams transitioning to AI tools.

Organisational support structures—including transparent communication about AI implementation, career development pathways, and job security assurances—are critical for mitigating job insecurity that undermines team psychological safety and knowledge-sharing.

Leaders should proactively address job insecurity concerns through clear messaging about role evolution rather than elimination, as unaddressed anxiety about automation dampens the psychological safety needed for employees to experiment with and openly discuss AI capabilities.

articles.title: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — full article details needed to assess sample size, geographic scope, and sector representation. Nature publishes diverse methodologies; generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title.
takeaways: Monitor and assess how AI adoption is affecting employees' emotional experiences at work — negative affective well-being may signal psychological safety concerns that need addressing before productivity suffers.

When introducing AI tools, deliberately create space for employees to voice concerns and anxieties about the technology without fear of judgment or repercussion — this is a key psychological safety intervention during AI transitions.
Consider that AI's impact on affective well-being may vary by role and context — tailor support and change management strategies rather than assuming uniform effects across the organisation.
